\[
p_\theta(t) = \sum_{x \cos\theta - y \sin\theta\, =\, t} I(x, y),
\quad
\theta_i = \frac{180^\circ\, i}{n},
\qquad
Q_i = h * p_{\theta_i},
\quad
\hat{I}(x, y) = \frac{\pi}{2n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} Q_i(x \cos\theta_i - y \sin\theta_i),
\qquad
n = 180
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I(x, y)\): The input channel, with x to the right and y downward from the middle
- \(p_\theta(t)\): The projection at angle theta, at position t along the detector
- \(n, \theta_i\): The number of angles and the angles themselves
- \(h\): The ramp filter, times the window
- \(Q_i\): The filtered projection at angle theta_i
- \(\hat{I}\): The rebuilt channel

The Radon transform p_theta(t) sums the image along the line at angle theta and distance t from the middle. Stacking the projections for all angles gives the sinogram. A point turns into a sine curve there, which gives the sinogram its name. The Fourier slice theorem says that the 1-D Fourier transform of one projection is the slice of the 2-D Fourier transform of the image along the same angle. So the projections hold the whole spectrum, but the slices crowd together near the center and spread apart far from it. Plain back projection smears each projection back along its lines and sums them. That blurs the image, since low frequencies are counted too often. The ramp filter h, whose response grows with |frequency|, undoes this weighting. Here h is the sampled ramp filter of Kak and Slaney. It has h(0) = 1/4, h(k) = -1 / (pi k)^2 for odd k and 0 for even k. It is applied with the FFT and multiplied by the chosen window. x grows to the right and y downward from the middle.
